title: Are the contractors with overruns better connected?
question: Do contractors whose agreement grew by half or ran two years long lobby, give to campaigns, or carry warning signs more often than other contractors with Board-approved agreements?
finding: 192 contractors had such an agreement and 191 others in the same files did not. Lobbied City officials through a registered lobbyist: 13 of 192 (7%) against 12 of 191 (6%), a gap chance would give 51% of the time. Gave to a political committee in its own name: 21 of 192 (11%) against 15 of 191 (8%), a gap chance would give 20% of the time. Has staff who gave to candidates for City office: 69 of 192 (36%) against 40 of 191 (21%), a gap chance would give less than 0.1% of the time. Carries a warning sign elsewhere on this site: 86 of 192 (45%) against 52 of 191 (27%), a gap chance would give less than 0.1% of the time. So 2 of the four links are more common among the contractors with overruns than chance allows. But large nonprofits have their agreements extended most often, have the most staff to give, and are the organizations this site has examined most, so like has to be compared with like: nonprofit with nonprofit and business with business, in thirds by how much the City has paid them. Has staff who gave to candidates for City office: 69 with an overrun, where 67.7 would be expected from organizations of the same kind and size (chance 42%); among businesses alone 19 of 112 against 25 of 136. Carries a warning sign elsewhere on this site: 86 with an overrun, where 85.3 would be expected from organizations of the same kind and size (chance 48%); among businesses alone 27 of 112 against 21 of 136. Compared that way none of the gaps is beyond chance: the overlap reflects which kind and size of organization has its agreements extended, not better connections.
how: The two groups are every contractor with a Board-approved agreement that grew by half or ran two years past its first end date, and every other contractor with a measured Board agreement. Four links are counted by name: the contractor is the client in a registered lobbyist's report of a contact with a City official; it appears as a contributor in its own name in campaign filings (itemized contributions only, each counted once); people who give it as their employer contributed to committees of candidates for City office; and it carries a warning sign in the site's map of flagged payees (signs that only restate an amendment, an exception, a Board approval or a figure from these screens are left out, since they come from the same files). Each pair of shares is compared with a one-sided exact test, and then again within groups of the same kind (nonprofit or business) and size (thirds by City payments). Rows list the contractors with an overrun and at least one link; no person is named or counted individually.
limits: Lobbying is disclosed advocacy, and large contractors lobby about many things besides their contracts. City law bars a contractor and its officers from giving to an official who must approve its contract around the time of approval; gifts to ballot-measure committees, and gifts by ordinary employees on their own account, are what most of these are. Employer names are typed by donors and matched by spelling, so a match is a name match. A warning sign elsewhere is a lead that nobody has ruled on. A link in the same row as an overrun does not connect the two: no file read here ties a contribution or a contact to an amendment. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
